Thoughts of dread for the living. Pandering with the queen of sorrow. Pandering to the mirrors of no tomorrow.
Thoughts of dread for the living.
Pandering with the queen of sorrow.
Pandering to the mirrors of no tomorrow.

Depression can turn a trip to the corner shop into such a long negotiation with yourself that the place ends up closing long before you’ve picked up your keys. On “Feelings Are Monsters,” Berlin’s Night Nail give that dread seven eyes and seven legs. Brandon Robert counts them off as though taking inventory might make the damn thing easier to deal with.

Once upon a time, Robert was scraping by as a hired bassist in Hollywood, selling other people’s demos on the street, when a bandmate who put great stock in lucky numbers told him to “cheer up.” “It was degrading,” Robert says of those days. “But, we had to eat. Super dark times.”

“I decided that day to never play for someone else’s dream again,” Robert recalls. “I started recording my own music. I learned the hard way that no one tells your story for you. My bandmates actually did support me in my breakaway dream and ended up helping me tremendously with making my first singles and videos. But, I learned it’s really all on you to make it happen and rightfully so.”

That faith in lucky numbers has a sour afterlife in the refrain, where Robert sings, “Luck won’t change your number.” The track opens in a clatter, with bright flecks of guitar sticking out of the noise. Once the drums snap into time, the guitar winds through the sort of uneasy melody The Comsat Angels used to make sound inevitable, while the bassline lays down a gothic rock groove. A little over a minute in, Ruby Mai’s saxophone takes over from Robert’s low recitation. He comes back with his voice raised, then lets it sink in again, deeper, as he draws out his ode to the “queen of sorrow.” A rubbery bass break gives way to another round of counting before the guitar takes the song out.

Director Ilija Gavrilenko and editor Jean De Oliveira keep returning to the band under blue light, with black wisps spreading across the frame. Between those shots, a skull-faced figure in a wide black hat rides a lime-green scooter and lopes around a courtyard carpeted with fallen leaves. It looks like somebody sent a horror-movie ghoul out to run an errand.
Watch the video for “Feelings Are Monsters” below.

Night Nail formed in Los Angeles in 2013 and moved to Berlin before releasing their 2018 debut, LA Demons , on Cleopatra Records. March To Autumn followed on Cold Transmission in 2020, and Metropolis released Fates Explained in 2023. William Faith and Sven Wolff handled mixing and post-production on Night Nail’s fourth studio album, Infinite Fountain . There’s something profoundly rotten about a world where people can disappear, families can be destroyed, and the surviving witnesses are expected to carry on buying groceries and paying…
Though they’d lost control of the outskirts of their town
and I loathe to tell you how it ends
so in silence we bow our heads

There’s something profoundly rotten about a world where people can disappear, families can be destroyed, and the surviving witnesses are expected to carry on buying groceries and paying their miserable bills while history quietly buries the evidence. Human civilization has developed an extraordinary talent for committing atrocities, commemorating the dead, and finding fresh excuses to repeat the process. Somewhere in this grand procession of moral bankruptcy, Seattle’s Profit Prison has found sufficient inspiration to write a disco song about the unbearable weight of collective guilt.

The solo project of Parker Lautensleger, whose musical history includes Anteinferno, Bhereg, Victims Panel, and Excarnated Entity, has spent nearly a decade exploring the more psychologically disturbed possibilities of electronic pop. His latest single, In Memoriam, taken from the forthcoming album Why art thou wroth? And why is thy countenance fallen? , sounds like Bronski Beat wandering into a particularly unpleasant historical reckoning, with electronic pioneer Gershon Kingsley conducting the proceedings from behind an enormous bank of synthesizers.

The arrangement possesses a strange, almost indecent sweetness. Synthesizers trace delicate melodic figures above a measured electronic rhythm, their crystalline repetitions creating the impression of a forgotten European dance record rescued from somebody’s flooded basement. Lautensleger sings with a trembling, distant resignation, his voice occupying the uncomfortable space between Neil Young’s wounded sincerity and the exquisite emotional distress of early synthpop by Das Kabinette, Depeche Mode, and others you might find on the Some Bizzare Compilation. Every syllable seems burdened by information its owner would dearly prefer to forget.

And what dreadful information it is. The lyrics describe a family whose apparently stable existence has been overturned by events unfolding near a border, where some unspecified act of violence has left questions that nobody seems willing to answer. Children inherit uncertainty, the dead receive their solemn acknowledgments, and the living are forced to contemplate the possibility that their own moral identities have been built upon carefully maintained ignorance. The song’s repeated interrogations grow increasingly desperate, suggesting a confrontation with somebody whose participation in an atrocity has become impossible to dismiss. Beneath the delicate electronic flourishes lies the hideous proposition that ordinary people can commit extraordinary acts of cruelty and subsequently spend entire lifetimes inventing explanations for themselves.

In Memoriam ‘s synthesizers maintain their patient, hypnotic progression while the words wander into the ugliest corners of human responsibility. You could conceivably dance to this record, which raises some rather uncomfortable questions about the emotional usefulness of disco. Lautensleger leaves those questions unanswered, however, allowing the music to continue its beautiful, merciless rotations while the accumulated weight of memory threatens to crush everything beneath it.

The video takes on a philosophical matter, as though we’re prisoners in Plato’s cave, watching distorted projections of events whose true nature remains somewhere beyond our comprehension. The road stretches onward, the lights assault our vision, and every image seems to conceal a fragment of some dreadful revelation.

At the edge of the abyss I stand Into the depths I am drawn The future without me Troglobite in bizarre light.
At the edge of the abyss I stand

A red light in a fog-filled nightclub lets you see who’s beside you on the dance floor. In a limestone cave, a lamp can reveal an olm, a pale salamander that lives underground. For Hanover-based “singer-doomwriter” David Barteczko , who first played as KOSMOBERKH on an open stage in Oldenburg, there’s a kinship between those two kinds of light. He puts them side by side on Troglobiten in Absonderlicht , a title he translates as “Troglobites in Secluded Light.”

Released November 6, 2026, on Barteczko’s own Zeichenlos Records , the ten-track album is his first since 2018’s oneiroi , which came out under the name Mosaikh . A club gives young people somewhere to make things together and try out how they want to live. Barteczko’s characters are looking for that kind of room under political and economic pressure. Pandemic isolation, war, a changing climate and the lure of conspiracy theories and parallel lives online form the backdrop to the album’s loosely connected episodes.

That first stage was Craftwork Café at Oldenburg’s Metro discotheque, where Barteczko tried out songs between 2011 and 2013. He describes those sets in terms of Stravinsky’s The Rite of Spring and Joy Division’s “Dead Souls,” both evoked by a single acoustic guitar. The 2014 demo Urbild began his recording partnership with Alex Pojda . Barteczko set his voice aside for the instrumental post-rock of Dim Nachttag in 2016 and took up singing again with Mosaikh, the electric trio whose songs about belonging drew on his experience as a Polish migrant.

During the break from KOSMOBERKH, Barteczko played in prog-doom band CMDR RIKR and post-rock group BRUECKEN. He returned to the stage in May 2024, opening for Extra Life at Cadillac in Oldenburg with cellist Jann Michael Engel , whose credits include Anne Clark and Mila Mar. The pair recorded the cello in Göttingen, and Barteczko tracked his vocals, synths, percussion and effects at home. Most of the guitars were recorded at Holodeck Studio, where Pojda co-produced the album with Barteczko and mixed and mastered it.

Barteczko’s acoustic guitar and Engel’s cello are at the center of the record. Synths, electronic percussion and field recordings carry the arrangements into ethereal wave and chamber doom. Barteczko’s reference points range from early Dead Can Dance and Scott Walker’s Scott 4 to David Bowie’s The Man Who Sold the World and Peter Hammill’s In Camera .

Deep strums and a low cello line set the instrumental “Fiz Oblon” in motion. The opener, issued October 16 as the fourth and final advance single, has the pace of a walk by lantern light, with the drums moving steadily beneath the acoustic riffs and Alex Pojda’s bass carrying the rounded weight of gothic rock. Engel takes the cello higher against the guitar before a rubbery industrial darkwave beat takes over for a spell. The cello returns to pick up the melody. The piece is named for the Bippen discotheque where Barteczko developed his taste in music, and he dedicates it to the memory of Pai and Hage. In the single notes, he credits clubs like this one with bringing him to music and to people who stayed in his life.

Barteczko first sings on “Asche meiner Jugend,” in a high, unhurried voice over gentle acoustic guitar. The lyric puts crimson clouds in a skylight and stroboscopes in a room he once knew. He can picture it well enough to feel like a stranger there now. Reverb carries off the ends of his phrases in the chorus, and Engel comes in with a low, grieving cello line. The two instruments find a brisk folk rhythm as Barteczko sings with more force. The quicker rhythm gives him a few bars to dance on the ashes of his youth and ask if anyone can see him glow.

A light chime moves through “Sterngeworden” like bells attached to someone’s dancing feet. More than 200,000 Carbon Monoxide Detectors Are Being Recalled Due to the Risk of “Serious Injury or…
Around 210,000 carbon monoxide detectors are being recalled because they don't properly detect dangerous levels of carbon monoxide.

Some recalls are more serious than others, and this is a serious one. More than 210,000 carbon monoxide and natural gas detectors are being recalled because they can fail to alert consumers to dangerous levels of carbon monoxide , potentially putting people at risk of serious injury or death.
The U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) announced the recall on Wednesday, Nov. 25, involving Steadfast Haven 4-in-1 plug-in CO and natural gas detectors sold by Zenara Commerce LLC.
What consumers need to know about the recall
So, how do you know if you have an affected device? Here’s the scoop.

The recall covers models KH158 and GC03, with approximately 210,410 units affected. The KH158 model is round in shape. It comes in gray or white plastic housing with a black digital display. Meanwhile, the GC03 model is rectangular with a black housing and a black digital display. Consumers can find the model number on the white label on the back of the device, right near the plug.
Consumers purchased the detectors online at Truststeadfast.com between February 2026 and September 2026. They cost around $48 to $70.

The biggest concern is that these devices may not sound an alarm when hazardous levels of carbon monoxide are present. Carbon monoxide is particularly dangerous because it is odorless and colorless, making a functioning detector an important safety device in the home.
According to the CPSC, Zenara has received one report of a detector failing to alarm during a carbon monoxide leak. No injuries have been reported, however.

Consumers should contact Zenara immediately to request a free replacement. The company is asking customers to register at www.truststeadfast.com/pages/recall , mark the recalled detector with the word “RECALLED” and their initials using permanent marker, then upload a photo of the marked product.
Consumers should continue using their recalled detectors until the replacement is installed. Once registration is confirmed, they should dispose of the recalled unit in their household trash.

For additional information, consumers can email recall@truststeadfast.com or visit the company’s recall website. Given the potential consequences, this is one recall homeowners won’t want to overlook.

Nearly a month after the beloved actor’s death at age 86, Avengers: Doomsday directors Joe and Anthony Russo opened up about what it was like working with Stewart as he reprised his iconic role of Professor Charles Xavier one last time.

The upcoming Marvel blockbuster, which hits theaters Dec. 18, will mark Stewart’s final onscreen performance. And according to the Russo brothers, the actor’s dedication to his craft was particularly moving given the health challenges he was facing behind the scenes.
Patrick Stewart’s health struggles made filming Avengers: Doomsday especially emotional

Speaking with Entertainment Weekly in a piece shared Nov. 24, Anthony recalled how determined Stewart was to give his fellow cast and crew members the best possible experience despite his declining health. “It was clear that he was struggling with his health, and he worked so hard to deliver a performance and a presence—for us as directors, for his other actors, for the crew,” Anthony said.

The director explained that Stewart’s commitment went far beyond what was typically expected of an actor arriving on set. “For him to have muscled through and delivered the performance that he did in that movie, and the experience that he delivered for all of us as collaborators, it made it intensely emotional.”

Stewart’s family announced his death on Oct. 29, revealing that the actor had died from Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia .

Although Marvel initially offered Stewart roles in both Avengers: Doomsday and its 2027 sequel, Avengers: Secret Wars , he opted to appear only in the former. His final performance will also feature an emotional scene about forgiveness opposite longtime friend and fellow X-Men star Ian McKellen, who returns as Magneto.
Feige confirmed that Marvel is currently exploring ways to commemorate Stewart in the upcoming film. “We’re looking now at how we can put something together that honors and respects our friend.”

12 Common Holiday-Party Disasters—And How to Fix Them ASAP
From kitchen mishaps to awkward moments with guests, even the most carefully planned celebration can go awry. Here's how to keep your cool and save the day.

I entertain a lot around the holidays, and I mean a lot: an annual party with former work colleagues; a Hanukkah dinner (I’m not Jewish, but my crew love latkes); a homemade-pizza night and gingerbread-house-building session with my niece, her BFF and their moms; and, of course, the Feast of the Seven Fishes, the Italian American Christmas Eve tradition .

I’m a planner, and an incredibly organized one, at that. I’ve got spreadsheets with shopping lists, ingredient lists, detailed to-do lists … you get the picture. And yet, no matter how prepared I am, things happen. Like the time I dropped a baking dish of perfectly browned, crispy-edged roasted potatoes on my tile floor, or the time—or, should I say, times?—I ran out of ice. Because here’s the thing: Holiday-party disasters are inevitable. You can plan for every possible scenario, but eventually something will go sideways. And when it does, well, the party must go on.

The trick is knowing how to recover without turning a minor snafu into a major production. As event planner Renee Patrone Rhinehart puts it, “Your guests probably have no idea something went wrong until you start announcing it to everyone.” Her advice? “Just roll with it!”

To find out how to roll with a dozen of the most common holiday-party disasters when you’re hosting , I went to the experts. Iron Chef Alex Guarnaschelli and renowned Southern chef Carla Hall weigh in on turkey troubles and other food emergencies; event planners Rhinehart and Marcy Blum share their secrets for keeping a party on track; etiquette expert Myka Meier offers advice for navigating awkward social situations; and licensed marriage and family therapist Nari Jeter, PhD, weighs in on emotionally charged moments.

So whether your turkey is taking forever to cook, an unexpected guest arrives or your uncle decides today is the perfect time to reignite that family feud, here’s how to save the celebration—and your sanity. Party on!

You’re still getting dressed, the kitchen is a disaster zone, and the appetizers aren’t even out yet. Then the doorbell rings—20 minutes before you expected anyone. Now you need to switch into host mode, and fast.

What to do: Welcome them warmly, offer a drink , and, if you’re comfortable, give them a small task, like putting on the music or lighting candles. “You’re early! Perfect timing. Grab a drink, and help me finish up!” is a perfectly acceptable response, says Rhinehart. My friends know that’s the case at my house: You show up early, and I’m putting you to work.

(For what it’s worth: Meier notes that guests should arrive at the stated time for a seated dinner; for a more casual gathering, arriving 10 to 15 minutes after the start time is generally appropriate.)

Why it works: You don’t need to drop everything to entertain an early arrival. A little hospitality goes a long way, and giving someone a simple job can make them feel included rather than in the way. It can even turn into a bonding moment with your new guest!

You planned dinner for eight, set the table for eight and made just enough food for eight. Then someone shows up with an unexpected plus-one. You could panic about the extra chair and plate, or you could get creative and make it work.

What to do: Take a breath , pull up an extra chair and welcome that person as though you expected them all along. “As a host, your goal is to make everyone feel welcome, even when you’re caught off guard,” says Meier. Simply say, “How lovely to meet you! Come on in.” After all, she adds, “It was not the guest’s fault they were asked to be there, and you don’t want them to feel that when arriving.”

Blum says to have card stock and a pen on hand to make an extra place card, if necessary. Rhinehart recommends stretching the meal with whatever you have—bread, salad or an extra side—and resisting the urge to announce that you weren’t prepared for another person.

Why it works: You’re taking charge, being an excellent hostess and rolling with the surprise. Making a fuss, on the other hand, can turn a small logistical hiccup into an awkward moment. As Rhinehart says, “Nobody needs to know!”

Is It Really Rude to Opt Out of the Gift Exchange?
The anxiety—and financial pressure—of getting a present for a group gift swap can feel exhausting during an already overscheduled season. Can you just skip it? The post Is It Really Rude to…

Like all torturous extended family traditions, ours started with good intentions. One year, someone got left off the list during our chaotic annual Christmas gift free-for-all. Feelings were hurt. So being responsible adults, we fixed the problem by inventing an entire bureaucracy: the Official Family Gift Exchange.

The idea was fine. The rules were what ruined us. It started with just drawing names. Then we added a price limit. Then a price minimum, after somebody’s “gift” turned out to be an already-opened bottle of lotion. Then a rule requiring you to talk to your assigned person about their interests, which metastasized into a 15-question survey, then into a shared spreadsheet, tracked with the rigor of a Pentagon budget.

Then the “ no regifting ” clause. Then the Great Gift Card Debate, which raged for years: Do gift cards even count as real gifts? Does one to a specific store outrank a Visa card? Does it have to be taped to something ­wrappable, or are we now just handing each other receipts?

It all came to a head the year my husband’s gift got returned to him. Not regifted— returned, like a defective toaster , with a note that it wasn’t thoughtful enough. Being an eternal optimist, he tried again. That gift also came back, this time via USPS, meaning the recipient paid actual postage to send it away rather than keep it one more day. That’s when we knew we wanted out. It wasn’t working anymore.

My husband and I decided to pull the plug. No elaborate exchange, just a gift card to each family, no survey required. What had started as a fun, generous tradition had somehow turned into a monthlong hostage situation that began every November.

Naturally, quitting had consequences: The following year, someone anonymously (although I’m pretty sure I know who) sent us a calendar of dogs pooping. (Yes, that’s a thing. And yes, you can buy it. I do not recommend gifting it, though I also cannot stop thinking about the person who decided the world needed it as a wall calendar.)

It’s not just my family that has a hard time managing this. More often than not, gift exchanges—office, family or friend group—start as a fun idea but end up being a spreadsheet with hurt feelings. So is opting out of the whole enterprise actually rude?

Financially, gift exchanges have quietly inflated like everything else. A $10 white elephant gag gift is now a $25-and-up “guideline” that creeps to $40 the second someone brings a nice candle. Multiply that by the office exchange, the neighborhood exchange and the family swaps, and you’re out $200 before buying anything for someone you actually live with. And, it must be said, in this economy?

There are also the plain logistics: Exchanges take time most of us don’t have in December. Saying no to one more obligation isn’t a personality flaw; it’s functioning boundaries. And if the group’s response to “I’ll sit this one out” is outrage, that says more about their expectations than your manners.

If only it were that easy. Gift swaps, especially the family and friend kind, aren’t really about the gift. They’re a shared ritual , and rituals only work if everyone shows up. Opt out and you can shift the whole dynamic—an odd number of ornaments, a recalculated spreadsheet, or Grandma noticing the empty spot under the tree and asking about it at dinner, forever.

There’s also the momentum problem. Once one person opts out “just this year,” the tradition can quietly die. If the exchange genuinely matters to the group, your exit—however ­reasonable—can be the beginning of the end for people who looked forward to it.

Context is everything, and office, family and friend exchanges are not all the same animal. Office exchanges are the easiest to skip—it’s a workplace, not a family reunion, and “I’m sitting this one out” needs zero explanation. Unless, of course, your boss makes it mandatory.

Somewhere between untangling last year’s Christmas lights and realizing you somehow signed up to bring three sides to Thanksgiving, the festive spirit can start to feel a little MIA. What is the Holiday Wish Line?

First launched in December 2023, the Holiday Wish Line features prerecorded messages from children who have had their wishes granted by Make-A-Wish. Think jokes, holiday songs, personal stories and the kind of words of encouragement that somehow hit differently when they come from a kid.
This year, the hotline opened on Nov. 23, just in time for the Thanksgiving rush . Anyone nationwide can call (480) 914-9474 (WISH) through Dec. 31.
Before you dial, take a peek behind the scenes . Watching a group of Gen Alphas try to figure out a rotary phone might make you feel a little old, but it’s also the cutest thing you’ll see all week.

This year’s lineup is part reunion and part debut. Seven of the nine have lent their voices to the hotline before, and two are brand-new. Every one of them has faced a major health battle and dreamed big anyway. Here’s how their wishes came true:

And with Giving Tuesday landing on Dec. 1, there’s no better time to pay a little kindness forward .

I pulled up some old photos on my phone—snaps of pictures that used to live in albums at the center of my parents’ living room. We started taking guesses about when they were from and shared stories about what was happening in them. We both remembered family picnics at the waterfall, our dog Cujo (yes, Cujo), and flying kites in the cornfield across the house. But there were people, places and stories I couldn’t recall at all, like a close family friend’s house we spent a lot of time at; my sister could still describe it in detail.
That’s when it hit me: It had been years since we’d flipped through old albums like that. As physical albums get left behind and older relatives depart, we’re increasingly losing our family history.

I’ve researched bits of my family’s genealogy over the years, but I’ve always run into roadblocks. Like many families in the U.S., our ancestors immigrated several generations ago, and a lot of details were lost or changed along the way. How do you document family history when there are so many missing pieces? By tackling it little by little, says Allison Singleton, the genealogy services manager at the Genealogy Center. “There will be gaps of information you don’t know,” she says. But don’t let that stop you.

That being said, you’ll have a lot more luck if you have a method to the madness. That’s why I reached out to a few experts who do this for a living and could lay it out in simple terms for us. In addition to Singleton, I spoke with Kyle Betit, a senior genealogist at Ancestry; Haleh Shoa, a certified professional photo organizer and the founder of Picturli; and Peter Andrew Wint, the founder of Family Roots.

It turns out, there are a lot of strategies and resources available, and some of them are free. Read on to find out how to document family history , create a family tree and be the detective your clan needs—starting now!
How on earth do you even start this kind of project?
Before you dive into documenting your family’s history, determine your goal. “Knowing where you want to end up tells you where to start and how much you need to gather,” Shoa says.

Next, collect supplies. Shoa says you’ll need several plastic bins, colorful index cards for categorizing batches of photos, an archival pencil, a 2TB or 4TB external hard drive for storage, nitrile gloves for handling photos, and a notebook or spreadsheet for tracking.

Then, gather the documentation you already have and group it into categories. Think of this like taking an inventory. “Put like with like,” Shoa says. “The albums, the slides, the negatives and the VHS tapes should each have their own piles.” In addition to photos and videos, include things like old letters , newspaper clippings, obituaries, birth and death certificates, and recipe cards. “These items are full of clues about your family history,” Singleton notes. After you’ve grouped everything, you’ll dig into each category. (More on that below.)

Keep in mind that you don’t need to do everything at once. “Start small—with one photograph, one document, one family story, one person or one question—and see how your research progresses,” Singleton advises. After all, you don’t want to get overwhelmed before you even really start!
How do you create a family tree?
To create a family tree, gather and cross-check details about your family, and designate a place to keep it all organized. Follow these steps to get started.
Building your tree online allows you to save and share it virtually, and on some platforms, you can turn on collaborative permissions so relatives can contribute in real time.

If you’re looking for a free and simple platform that’s particularly good for beginners, Shoa recommends Family Echo. You can also create a basic free tree in FamilySearch, Canva, Ancestry and MyHeritage. Just be aware that free trees may have limitations, and access to some records and services may require a paid subscription.

How to Navigate Grief During the Holidays in Ways You’ll Actually Find Helpful
When the season feels anything but merry, these expert tips will give you a game plan to make it through—even when that feels impossible.

No matter what time of year you’ve lost someone, navigating that grief during the season devoted to joy, togetherness and sparkle can become a challenge unto itself. When my 82-year-old mom died the night before Thanksgiving three years ago, my grief became permanently imprinted into the holidays. Ever since, I’ve swung between wanting to eat cookies by the fire with Santa and scream through the streets with Krampus.

The holidays haven’t felt the same since, and admittedly, I even feel a little dread around this time of the year. I’m not alone. According to American Psychiatric Association’s Healthy Minds poll from 2025 about holiday-related concerns, nearly half of adults polled felt worry over grief and missing someone . The reality is that the best parts of the season can lead to some of the worst feelings of loss.

There is no easy answer here, unfortunately, but experts do have a few suggestions to help people handle grief during the holidays . For that advice, I spoke with Raman Mohabir, PhD, a licensed professional clinical counselor and the founder of Good Mourning Mental Health Counseling, and Tess Clarkson, an end-of-life doula and the creator of the Your Best Goodbye workshop.
Read on to find out how to get through the holidays after a loss , find special ways to honor your loved ones and maybe even enjoy the season again.
Why are the holidays particularly hard after a loss?

First of all, it’s not your imagination: The holidays are harder. And the first notes of a familiar holiday song or the scent of a special dish can really feel like a gut punch. “The holiday season can further magnify grief because it is a time often marked with moments meant to be spent with family and loved ones, which can further highlight the absence of the person who has died,” Mohabir says . On top of that, you may feel guilt, anger or resentment for not feeling celebratory, and your grief can feel darker against all the sparkle.

How it hits can also depend on the kind of loss. Grief isn’t only about death, Mohabir notes. It can also include “ambiguous losses, such as the anticipatory grief associated with the decline of a loved one facing a terminal diagnosis, or loss due to divorce, deployment, incarceration or a miscarriage.” Those losses can be especially lonely during the holidays. “These ambiguous and disenfranchised grief experiences can complicate the holiday season as well, especially if the loss is not acknowledged or supported by others,” she says.
Whatever kind of loss you’re carrying, feeling as if you’re living a different holiday than everyone around you can be alienating.
Should you still celebrate the holidays after a loss?

It really depends on you. “There is no correct answer or moral obligation to how an individual should navigate the holiday season,” says Mohabir. A lot of it boils down to how you feel and who will be around you . Spending time with people who share your loss, or who are simply supportive, can be a real comfort and worth the effort. Spending it with people who aren’t supportive can do more harm than good, whether they’re friends or family.

“It is important to assess the quality of the support around you and what you need when gathering with others,” Mohabir says. Time alone counts too. “Choosing solitude and privacy can be restorative and healing as well,” she adds.

If celebrating feels like too much this year, try a gentler approach: “observing” the season or focusing on getting through it rather than celebrating it. “Maybe it is not putting up the tree or getting out the menorah,” Clarkson says. It’s also not all or nothing; Show up for dessert, pop by Christmas morning—”it’s about having more serenity without the performance of the holidays,” she says.
How should you approach the holiday season after a loss?

Start by listening to yourself rather than to your list of obligations. There’s no single right way to do the holidays while grieving. “It’s not a one-size-fits-all,” Clarkson says. “It behooves us to listen to ourselves for what we need.” That might be a walk, a good cry or a quiet night in, she says, or it might be more appointments with the therapist or a grief support group.

Priscilla Presley revealed the hilarious story behind her throwback photo
A post shared by Priscilla Presley (@priscillapresley)

Priscilla explained what the couple—who were married from 1967 to 1973—had been doing when the picture was taken. “Elvis and I were watching Hawaiian dancers at an outdoor lounge,” she wrote, dating the photograph to sometime in the 1970s.

This Junk-Drawer Staple Could Save Your Home in Case of Flooding, According to a New Study
A new study found that a surprisingly effective and cheap household tool blows sandbags out of the water when it comes to flood protection.

Flooding often brings to mind springtime thunderstorms and late-summer hurricanes, but this year, El Niño is serving up a nasty winter across much of the United States. Heavy rains and flooding are in the forecast for huge swaths of the country, leaving many wondering what they would do if water was bearing down.

Sandbags have been the go-to for centuries, but if you’ve ever tried to use them, you know they are a pain: heavy, labor-intensive and often not available when you need them. But now, researchers looking for inexpensive ways to help homeowners fight flooding have stumbled across something that blows sandbags out of the water.

Britain’s University of Hull released the surprising findings in a new report, and we have the results ahead. It turns out that something you no doubt have rattling around in your junk drawer or garage toolbox works better than sandbags—a lot better. Read on to learn an effective (and cheap) way to protect your home during a flood.
What junk-drawer staple can save your home from flooding?

That’s according to a new report called Testing the Performance of Low-cost, Temporary Property Flood Resilience (PFR) Solutions . The university teamed up with Flood Re, a partnership between the U.K. government and insurers, to pinpoint inexpensive ways for homeowners to protect their homes during a flood.

The results were amazing: Duct tape reduced water leakage 97% to 98% compared to a plain closed door. The much less common synthetic rubber tape (aka putty tape) did even better, with a 99% reduction. Even the worst-performing tape, yellow plastic tape, kept out 80% of simulated floodwaters during testing. And every single tape tested did better than sandbags, which reduced water intrusion by only 70%.

“Sandbags remain a symbol of flood protection , but these tests turn that assumption on its head,” said Jonathan Kassian, head of flood resilience at Flood Re. “What we have found is that some relatively simple and affordable products can do a much better job of keeping water out.”
Why does this work better than a sandbag?

For one thing, sandbags are porous, and they’re not designed to keep out water completely. Think of them more as a diversion tactic or obstruction, as opposed to tape, which can actually seal an opening through which water can flow.

In this study, researchers found that when placed in flood conditions of 0.2 meters (about 8 inches), sandbags leaked water at a mean rate of 584 liters per hour per meter, or 47 gallons per hour per foot. They were more effective in deeper water, but still only prevented, at most, 70% of water leakage . Sandbags are also heavy, time-intensive to deploy and difficult to place correctly.

Tape, on the other hand, is cheap and easy to store. It can be applied directly across gaps and conforms to irregular surfaces and openings where water can seep in. After the storm, cleanup is easy because tape is safely disposable, unlike sandbags, which absorb dangerous floodwater contaminants. And remember: Duct tape was more than 97% effective.
There is one caveat. Researchers concluded that how the tape was applied was “critical.” We’ll give you those details next.
How do you do this properly?

First, it’s important to understand that this was a research study about the effectiveness of certain barriers under testing conditions, not a how-to manual of using tape to stop a flood. But scientists were encouraged by the findings. Here are recommendations from the report:
Use a strong, wide tape. For duct tape, researchers recommend a width of 100 mm (roughly 4 inches).
Apply it to the flood-facing side. Tape performed best when it was applied on the outside of the door.

Cover vertical joints first. Tape the sides, making sure the vertical strip is attached to both the door and jamb and extends to the threshold. Then do the threshold and corners, overlapping the vertical strip.
Apply to clean, dry doors. To get the best adhesion, tape the door before wet weather arrives .
Make sure there are no openings. Avoid folds, press out any air bubbles and cover gaps.

That Sinking Feeling: A Race Against Time to Save a Pregnant Woman from a Car Submerged in Freezing Waters
A dazed pregnant woman drives into an ice-cold pond. Amid a sea of bystanders, one man takes action to save her life.

Shedly Apollon was awakened by a sound she couldn’t possibly sleep through: that of her car splashing into a pond … with her in it. Add in the rush of cold water pooling beneath her feet, and suddenly Apollon was fully alert, if disoriented. She was also fearing for her life. Actually, two lives. Apollon was in her 34th week of pregnancy on that cold morning this past February in Stuart, Florida, when she awoke to the reality that she was trapped in a sinking car .

Apollon, of nearby Port St. Lucie, had been on her way to a prenatal massage gifted by her fiancé, Woodly Sully. It was a birthday present. (Yes, this happened on Apollon’s 29th birthday.) Apollon had been struggling during her third trimester with preeclampsia, and as she drove to the massage, she began to feel woozy. She pulled her silver 2019 Hyundai Elantra over to the shoulder of Interstate 95, called Sully to let him know what was happening, drank some water, ate a little food and waited for the dizziness to subside.

After it did, about 10 minutes later, she got back on the road, but what happened next is a blur. Her car’s safety systems were beeping, telling her she was veering outside her lane, although in her haze-filled mind she was driving perfectly straight. She tried to pull over again, but started passing out. “I thought the car was in park,” Apollon recalls, “but in reality, it was still in drive.” And she drove off the right side of the road, straight into the pond.

When she came to seconds later to the sound of the splash, she unsnapped her seat belt and hit redial on her phone, then screamed to her confused fiancé, “I’m in a lake!” Within seconds, the call dropped. She and her unborn baby were all alone in a car that was listing, front driver’s side first, into a body of water.

Around this time, 29-year-old sport fisherman Logan Hayes of Sebastian, Florida, was driving down the same stretch of I-95 in his pickup, remarking to his friend and boss in the passenger seat, Chase Cornell, about how unusual it was that traffic was light and that they were running 20 minutes ahead of schedule on their work errand. “Something’s gonna happen,” Hayes joked.
Sure enough, Hayes soon saw brake lights ahead of him. And then the reason for the sudden slowdown: the Elantra, barely floating in the water.

Other cars had pulled over, but so far nobody had gotten out to help. So Hayes, also a professional surfer and confident swimmer, crossed from the far left lane across two other lanes, cutting off every car in his way, then pulled onto the shoulder and leaped out of the truck.
“Hey, is someone in that car?” he asked a bystander.

Hayes ran 50 yards down the highway, then a few more feet to the water’s edge, his eyes fixed on the Elantra. He was shedding clothing every step of the way. Off came his hat, his sunglasses, his shirt, his fishing boots, his sweatpants, his socks … until all he had on were his board shorts.

The outdoor temperature was in the mid-40s when Hayes hit the water around 8 a.m., and the pond was colder than that. But Hayes was surging with adrenaline and didn’t feel the chill as he dove in , trying to cover the distance as quickly as he could. He was underwater for a couple of seconds, then came up and took a few more strokes, and he was at the car.

With the vehicle tipping forward and to the left, the rear passenger door was the only one not submerged. Treading water, he pulled on the door handle, and it flew open. Scared and still struggling to get her bearings, Apollon was jolted by the sight of Hayes floating just outside her suddenly wide-open back door. “You have to get out of the car right now!” he yelled to her.
“You need to!” he urged. “You need to get to me.”

Apollon saw she’d have to crawl over the console between the seats—not easy to do in a car listing in the opposite direction, especially as her instinct was to move delicately and protect her belly. She swung her legs around so her feet were pointing toward Hayes. Now lying on her side, she pushed with her arms and slid up the console, inching toward the back seat, gravity working against her at every turn.

How a Thanksgiving Crisis Inspired the Invention of Swanson’s TV Dinner (1953)
“Taste — the mouth’s response to the sensation of eating and drinking — is a strange and complex and complicated thing,” writes New York Times food editor Craig Claiborne. “I am convinced…

“Taste — the mouth’s response to the sensation of eating and drinking — is a strange and complex and complicated thing,” writes New York Times food editor Craig Claiborne . “I am convinced that there are a multitude of people (Americans, mostly, to judge by the people who buy TV dinners and frozen pizzas) who have no taste whatsoever.” That column was published almost exactly 50 years ago, but even at that point, such convenience-oriented food products had already enjoyed prominence in American life for two decades. Though it could hardly have made a dent in the popularity of TV dinners, Claiborne’s typically waspish aside did draw a letter of objection from one Rosalie Levine of Lakewood, California.

“I live alone, I must control my weight. I am not a skilled cook,” she writes. The TV dinner’s price “cannot possibly be bettered”; what’s more, “each oven-ready dinner takes only half an hour’s worth of gas to prepare, and there are no pots or pans to clean up afterward.” While none of these advantages were accidental, the oft-told story of the concept’s emergence begins with a corporate crisis.

“In 1953, someone at Swanson colossally miscalculated the level of the American appetite for Thanksgiving turkey, leaving the company with some 260 tons of frozen birds,” as Smithsonian.com’s Owen Edwards tells it . “Inspired by the trays of pre-prepared food served on airlines,” Swanson salesman Gerry Thomas set the machinery in motion to package the unwanted meat with gravy and sides like cornbread and sweet potatoes, ready for stocking in America’s frozen-food aisles.

The following year, Swanson sold ten million such “TV dinners,” a name attributed to both the shape of the boxes and the form of entertainment families tended to enjoy while eating the meals within. “In 1950, only 9 percent of U.S. households had television sets — but by 1955, the number had risen to more than 64 percent, and by 1960, to more than 87 percent,” writes Kovie Biakolo in a more recent Smithsonian piece . (Among the Smithsonian Institution’s holdings, incidentally, is an original Swanson TV dinner tray .) Another breakthrough came with the introduction of microwave-safe trays, bringing total preparation time under ten minutes. During the COVID-19 pandemic, Americans rekindled their love affair with frozen meals, “spending nearly 50 percent more on them in April 2020 over April 2019.”

Where holiday and commercial lore intersect, the details tend to get complicated. Swanson’s TV dinner did have its precedents: the core technology for quick-freezing packaged foods was invented over a century ago by entrepreneur Clarence Birdseye (he of the Birds Eye peas Edwards remembers as “little cryogenic miracles”), and in the late 1940s, different companies planned or attempted to bring frozen meals to market under brands like Strato-Plates, FridgiDinners, and One-Eyed Eskimo. None of those names tapped into the technology transforming not just American mass culture, but also the American way of life. In the fifties, associations with television (and, indeed, with air travel) carried a kind of sophistication they certainly don’t have today. Perhaps Craig Claiborne would be pleased that Americans never quite accepted microwaved TV dinners as a substitute for the Thanksgiving meal; what he’d think of the food they order through their apps is another matter entirely.

Alice’s Restaurant. It’s now a Thanksgiving classic, and something of a tradition around here. Recorded in 1967, the 18+ minute counterculture song recounts Arlo Guthrie’s real encounter with the law, starting on Thanksgiving Day 1965. As the long song unfolds, we hear all about how a hippie-bating police officer, by the name of William “Obie” Obanhein , arrested Arlo for littering. (Cultural footnote: Obie previously posed for several Norman Rockwell paintings, including the well-known painting, “The Runaway,” that graced a 1958 cover of The Saturday Evening Post .) In fairly short order, Arlo pleads guilty to a misdemeanor charge, pays a $25 fine, and cleans up the thrash. But the story isn’t over. Not by a long shot.

Later, when Arlo (son of Woody Guthrie) gets called up for the draft, the petty crime ironically becomes a basis for disqualifying him from military service in the Vietnam War. Guthrie recounts this with some bitterness as the song builds into a satirical protest against the war: “I’m sittin’ here on the Group W bench ’cause you want to know if I’m moral enough to join the Army, burn women, kids, houses and villages after bein’ a litterbug.” And then we’re back to the cheery chorus again: “You can get anything you want, at Alice’s Restaurant.”
We have featured Guthrie’s classic during past years. But, for this Thanksgiving, we give you the illustrated version.

The Map of Ancient Philosophy: Animation Shows How Socrates, Aristotle, Confucius, the Buddha & Other Great…
Here on Open Culture, we’ve often featured the charming and informative posters of Domain of Science. Each one maps out a different field of knowledge: there’s biology, physics, chemistry…

Here on Open Culture, we’ve often featured the charming and informative posters of Domain of Science . Each one maps out a different field of knowledge: there’s biology , physics , chemistry , quantum physics , quantum computing , fungi , and many others besides. But with his latest map, Domain of Science creator Dominic Walliman has turned away from the scientific realm — or rather, he’s ventured into the larger intellectual territory out of which it emerged. His new Map of Philosophy , which he explains in the video above , includes schools of thought going all the way back to 600 BC, and thinkers from antiquity like Thales, Laozi, Confucius, and the Buddha, who lived and died before science as we know it.

That hardly means that they’ve become irrelevant today. There still exist societies described as Confucian or Buddhist, of course, but in the Western world, we’re more likely to refer back to — and, in many cases, have read a bit of — the work of Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle. “They basically laid the intellectual foundation of Western philosophy, science, and political thought,” says Walliman. (He also reminds us that it was Socrates who said that the unexamined life is not worth living, which “hits pretty hard in the age of the distraction economy.”)

Though often mentioned together, these three ancient Greeks occupy slightly different positions on the philosophical map, with Socrates closer to the land of ethics, Plato to metaphysics, and Aristotle to epistemology.

As Walliman explains, “epistemology studies knowledge: what it is, where it comes from, and also how it differs from faith or opinions,” while also seeking out its limits. Aristotle’s rigor in testing and organizing knowledge makes him, in a sense, one of the earliest scientists. Though his body of theory may no longer be our best means of understanding how the world works, his systematic pursuit of such an understanding set him apart from much of the ancient intellectual world. The islands off the coast of the map’s mainland represent subfields still actively explored today, like the philosophies of mind, language, politics, religion, and science — which, for all its prestige, remains as subject to philosophical inquiry as any other area of human endeavor. The map of philosophy shows us not a rarefied, mostly abandoned territory, but the place where we all live our lives, examined or otherwise.

25 Films Inspired by Edgar Allan Poe Online: The Fall of the House of Usher, The Tell-Tale Heart, and More
Rank the films inspired by Edgar Allan Poe, and several adaptations of “The Fall of the House of Usher” will almost certainly come near the top. At first glance, that story of a man paying…

Rank the films inspired by Edgar Allan Poe, and several adaptations of “The Fall of the House of Usher” will almost certainly come near the top. At first glance, that story of a man paying a visit to an old friend who lives with his twin sister in their family’s grand house — each of the latter three well advanced into a different process of deterioration — might seem too short, as well as too light on conflict to translate into a conventional screenplay. Yet it’s also full of cinematically irresistible images, from the somehow ruinous yet wholly intact titular mansion to the bloodily wretched sister throwing herself upon the terrified brother who entombed her alive while their ancestral home collapses around them.

Of the twenty or thirty versions of “The Fall of the House of Usher” so far made for the screen, the most celebrated remains the one Jean Epstein directed in 1928. Officially designating it as one of the “great movies,” Roger Ebert calls that picture’s vision of the great hall “one of the most haunting spaces in the movies. Its floor is a vast marble expanse, interrupted here and there by an item of furniture that seems dwarfed by the surrounding emptiness. An odd staircase rises from one distant corner. It is not impossible that this vision, in one of the best-known French surrealist films, inspired the designers of the great hall of Xanadu in Citizen Kane .”

The avant-garde filmmaking duo James Sibley Watson Jr. and Melville Webber (in collaboration with e. e. cummings, who contributed to the script) could hardly manage the same scale of production design for their own short adaptation of Poe’s story , which happened to come out the same year.

But the resulting Expressionist take on the material has also been highly acclaimed, and through this YouTube playlist of Poe films , you can experience not just both of them, but also other adaptations of “The Fall of the House of Usher” by idiosyncratic Czech animator Jan Švankmajer and B‑movie powerhouse Roger Corman . Sensitive to Poe’s sensationalist appeal and air of transgressive decadence, Corman ended up directing an eight-film “Poe cycle,” nearly all of which star Vincent Price.

It’s fair to say that no film actor is more closely associated with Poe than Price, a link Tim Burton celebrated in animation at the beginning of his career. Price even played the writer himself in An Evening with Edgar Allan Poe , a special from 1970 in which he recites “The Sphinx,” “The Cask of Amontillado,” “The Pit and the Pendulum,” and “The Tell-Tale Heart.” That last, the most screen-adapted Poe story of them all, also appears on the playlist in various forms: an early D. W. Griffith feature , the directorial debut of Jules Dassin , an animated short narrated by James Mason , a British psychological thriller , and a transposition into modern-day New Orleans . And if you haven’t had enough Poe after watching through all 25 of these films, consider watching the recent, well-received Fall of the House of Usher miniseries on Netflix — an entertainment platform that satisfies much the same appetites Poe’s stories have been feeding for nearly two centuries.

Marie Curie Became the First Woman to Win a Nobel Prize, the First Person to Win Twice, and the Only Person…
For most of scientific history, women who made contributions to various fields have been sidelined or ignored in favor of male colleagues, who reaped fame, professional recognition, and…

For most of scientific history, women who made contributions to various fields have been sidelined or ignored in favor of male colleagues, who reaped fame, professional recognition, and cash rewards that come with prestigious prizes like the Nobel. Cornell historian of science Margaret Rossiter coined the term “The Matilda Effect” to describe sexist bias in the sciences. Rossiter’s work and popular reappraisals like book-turned-film Hidden Figures have inspired other women in academia to search for forgotten female scientists, and to find them, literally, in footnotes .

When systematic discrimination limits opportunities for any group, those who do receive recognition, the exceptions to the rule, must often be truly exceptional to succeed. There has been little doubt, both in her lifetime and in the many decades afterward, that Marie Curie was such a person. Although forced to study science in secret at a clandestine “ Floating University ” in her native Poland—since the universities refused to admit women—Curie (born Marie Salomea Sklodowska in 1867) would achieve such renown in her field that she was awarded not one, but two Nobel Prizes.

Curie and her husband Pierre shared the Nobel Prize in Physics with Antoine Henri Becquerel, discoverer of radioactivity, in 1903. The second prize, in Chemistry, was hers alone in 1911, “in recognition of her services to the advancement of chemistry by the discovery of the elements radium and polonium, by the isolation of radium and the study of the nature and compounds of this remarkable element.” Curie was not only the first woman to win a Nobel, but she was also the first person to win twice, and the only person to win in two different sciences.

These are but a handful of achievements in a string of firsts for Curie: denied positions in Poland, she earned a Ph.D. in France, awarded the degree in 1903 by the Sorbonne , the same year she won her first Nobel. “Her examiners,” notes the site Famous Scientists , “were of the view that she had made the greatest contribution to science ever found in a Ph.D. thesis.” Three years later, after Pierre was killed in an accident, Marie was offered his professorship and became the first female professor at the University of Paris.

Curie succeeded not in the absence of, but in spite of the sexist obstacles placed in her path at nearly every stage in her career. After she received her doctorate, the Curies were invited to the Royal Institution in London. Only Pierre was permitted to speak. That same year, the Nobel Committee decided to honor only her husband and Becquerel. The Academy relented when Pierre protested. Curie fell victim to a wave of xenophobia and anti-Semitism (though she was not Jewish) that swept through France in the 1900s, most famously in the so-called “Dreyfus Affair.”

In 1911, the year of her second Nobel, Curie was passed over for membership in the French Academy of Sciences . It would take another 51 years before the first woman, Marguerite Perey, a former doctoral student of Curie, would be elected to that body. That same year, Curie was persecuted relentlessly by the French press, the public, and her scientific rivals after it was revealed that she had had a brief affair with physicist Paul Langevin, one of Pierre Curie’s former students.

But no matter how many men in positions of power wanted to deter Curie, there always seemed to be more influential scientists and politicians who recognized the supreme value of her work and the need to help her continue it. After her second Nobel Prize, her native country finally recognized her with the offer to direct her own laboratory in Warsaw. Curie turned it down to focus on directing the Curie Laboratory in the Radium Institute of the University of Paris, which she founded in 1914, a major achievement and, again, only a small part of her legacy.

Curie is known, of course, foremost for her exceptional scientific work, but also for opening doors for women in science all over the world, though much of that door-opening may only have happened decades after her death in 1934, and much of it hasn’t happened at all yet. Behold the Most Detailed Painting in History: The Ghent Altarpiece
These days, if you want to see a particular painting, you can almost certainly pull it up online in seconds. In more and more cases, the resolution of the image will be so high that you can…

These days, if you want to see a particular painting, you can almost certainly pull it up online in seconds. In more and more cases, the resolution of the image will be so high that you can zoom in and in and in: such a level of detail is unavailable in a museum, of course, but also difficult to access even if you owned the physical artwork in question. Here on Open Culture, we’ve previously featured such luxuriantly digitized paintings as The Night Watch , Girl with a Pearl Earring , and The Garden of Earthly Delights . But there’s at least one celebrated work of Dutch masters whose viewing experience can never truly be replicated on the internet: the Ghent Altarpiece , also called the Adoration of the Mystic Lamb , by Hubert and Jan van Eyck.

After watching the video from The Gaze above, you’ll surely want to take as close as possible a look at the online Ghent Altarpiece , seeking out such highlighted details as the individual hairs on Adam’s beard, the realistically awkward expressions on the faces of the angel chorus, and the identifiable crucifixion scene pinned to a pilgrim’s hat.

But that may only stoke your desire to make a pilgrimage of your own, to Belgium, where you can see the real thing carefully placed in St. Bavo’s Cathedral. In the early fifteenth century, when that institution was called St. John the Baptist’s Church, its warden was the wealthy merchant Jodocus Vijd. Having endowed a new chapel, Vijd also commissioned the van Eyck brothers to create an altarpiece spectacular enough to secure him a spot in the afterlife. The result was one of the earliest masterpieces of oil painting.

Even apart from that designation (to say nothing of its being the most stolen work of art in history ), it has enjoyed an impressive afterlife of its own. Of the many who have traveled to behold it in situ at St. Bavo’s, some have no doubt sought the ecstasy of faith that can only be felt in a true holy place. But others have been thrilled, whether they were aware of it beforehand, by all the attention the artists put into integrating the work with its surroundings. The light within its images, for example, is painted in such a way as to match the light streaming into the cathedral itself. Those who look closely at the gem worn by the foremost singing angel will see a reflection of the very room meant for the altar. By the time their eyes meet the knowing gaze of the sacrificial lamb, they’re all but guaranteed to have a religious experience — though whether its nature is Christian, artistic, or otherwise will depend, as it does with all enduring art, on the individual viewer.

How Isaac Newton Lost $3 Million Dollars in the “South Sea Bubble” of 1720: Even Geniuses Can’t Prevail…

The Aristotelian notion of “man” as a “rational animal” has seen its share of detractors, from the Cynics to Bertrand Russell to nearly the whole of Poststructuralist thought. Leave it up to Oscar Wilde to compress the debate between intellect and passion into a pithy aphorism: “Man is a rational animal who always loses his temper when he is called upon to act in accordance with the dictates of reason.”

We no longer need clever verbal barbs to refute too-optimistic assessments of human behavior. Economics is catching up: we have the language of neuroscience and psychology, which consistently tells us that humans decidedly do not behave rationally very often, but are driven by bias and biology in inexplicable ways . And for over a hundred years now, we’ve known that the clockwork Newtonian view of the physical universe turns out to be a much messier and indeterminate affair, as does the universe of the human mind.

Why, then, has so much economic theory operated with a kind of dogged Aristotelianism, insisting that the units of capitalist society, the workers, managers, investors, consumers, owners, renters, speculators, etc. behave in predictable ways? We have case after case showing that intelligence and critical reasoning often have little to do with success or failure in the market. In such cases, however, one often hears the “madness of crowds” or other clichés invoked as an explanation.

To illustrate, market reporters and business writers have seized upon the story of Isaac Newton’s spectacular rise and fall in the so-called “ South Sea Bubble ” of 1720. We find the story in Benjamin Graham’s 1949 classic The Intelligent Investor , a widely-read book that attributes the irrationality of market systems to an anthropomorphic entity named “Mr. Market.”

Back in the spring of 1720, Sir Isaac Newton owned shares in the South Sea Company, the hottest stock in England. Sensing that the market was getting out of hand, the great physicist muttered that he ‘ could calculate the motions of the heavenly bodies, but not the madness of the people .’ Newton dumped his South Sea shares, pocketing a 100% profit totaling £7,000. But just months later, swept up in the wild enthusiasm of the market, Newton jumped back in at a much higher price — and lost £20,000 (or more than $3 million in [2002–2003’s] money. For the rest of his life, he forbade anyone to speak the words ‘South Sea’ in his presence.

The quotation in bold may or may not have been uttered by Newton, but the events Graham describes did indeed happen. As the Wall Street Journal ’s Jason Zweig relates , University of Minnesota professor Andrew Odlyzko found that “Newton had shifted from a prudent investor with his money spread across several securities to a speculator who had plunged essentially all of his capital into a single stock. The great scientist was chasing hot performance as desperately as a day trader in 1999 or many bitcoin buyers in 2017.” (Odlyzko estimates Newton’s losses at closer to $4 million.) Perhaps it was not a metaphorical “Mr. Market” who cost Newton up to 77% “on his worst purchases,” nor was it widespread “wild enthusiasm”—the mass movement of passion that Enlightenment philosophers so feared.

Perhaps it was Newton himself who, Elena Holodny writes at Business Insider , “let his emotions get the best of him, and got swayed by the irrationality of the crowd.” Maybe it’s more accurate to say Newton succumbed to greed when the bubble expanded. “Throughout history,” Barbara Kollmeyer writes at Market Watch in her interview with author Richard Dale , “people—especially those at the top rung of society—have been greedy and gullible participants in financial bubbles. And Sir Isaac Newton was only human, after all.” (How many at the top rung of society fell prey to Bernie Madoff’s schemes? And a century before the South Sea Bubble , hundreds of wealthy investors lost their shirts in the Dutch Tulip Bulb craze. )

What Makes Notre-Dame Cathedral a Masterpiece of Gothic Architecture
And even upon learning that the most famous of all French cathedrals had been badly damaged rather than completely destroyed, it still felt as if something irreplaceable had been lost. It…

Most of us remember where we were when we heard that Notre-Dame had burned down. And even upon learning that the most famous of all French cathedrals had been badly damaged rather than completely destroyed, it still felt as if something irreplaceable had been lost. It made no difference whether we’d actually been to the place, as I hadn’t at the time. When I did finally make it to Paris four years later, Notre-Dame’s restoration was still underway, and construction walls prevented anyone from seeing much of anything at ground level, let alone entering. Yet crowds still gathered to take pictures in the square outside, apparently finding that proximity to such a civilizational landmark was enough, even in its partially ruined and inaccessible state.

Even without a chance to step inside, experiencing Notre-Dame’s surroundings on the Île de la Cité, as well as the greater urban context of Paris, certainly deepens one’s understanding of the beauty of the cathedral itself. So does visiting other, less widely known examples of the form, as shown by architecture-and-history YouTuber Manuel Bravo in his new video above .

Ordinary tourists in Paris may make a beeline for Notre-Dame, but they’re hardly likely to find their way out to the other medieval cathedrals in Saint-Denis, north of the city, much less all the way out in Laon. Though glorious in their own way, they’re perhaps even more valuable in providing the context of Gothic church architecture in which Notre-Dame made such a mark.

As Bravo explains it, Notre-Dame’s façade represents “the moment in which Gothic façade achieves its most balanced synthesis. The experiments and innovations of Saint-Denis and Laon are absorbed, disciplined, and unified into a composition in which no element appears arbitrary or independent from the whole.” Among its most influential appreciators was Victor Hugo, in whose time much of Paris’ Gothic architecture was being demolished. His romantic evocations of the medieval built environment in Notre-Dame de Paris (in English, The Hunchback of Notre-Dame ) helped save the much deteriorated titular structure, which received an ambitious renovation under Eugène Viollet-le-Duc between 1844 and 1864. That project went beyond period accuracy, adding such non-original details as the gallery of chimeras perched high enough to remain visible during the latest restoration work. Visitors today may notice that the interior doesn’t look exactly like it used to, but some will appreciate that even a monument like Notre-Dame must change with the centuries.

The Amazing Inventions of Ancient Greece: From Plato’s Alarm Clock to Ancient Flamethrowers
“It’s a sunny morning in ancient Greece. Students have started gathering in the Academy, but their famous teacher Plato is nowhere to be seen.” The great philosopher has, it seems…

“It’s a sunny morning in ancient Greece. Students have started gathering in the Academy, but their famous teacher Plato is nowhere to be seen.” The great philosopher has, it seems, “overslept and missed his own lecture.” The sun and the sound of early-rising animals may have failed Plato that day, as the story goes, but never would he let it happen again — at least after he got the mechanism worked out for the first alarm clock in history. Its design involves a series of containers linked by pipes through which water flows at a steady speed all night long. When the water accumulates in the penultimate, sealed vessel, air is pushed out through the flute embedded in its wall, producing something like birdsong.

Plato’s water alarm clock is just one of the pieces of advanced ancient Greek technology explained in the new video above from Lost in Time , a YouTube channel whose look at ancient Roman technology we posted here on Open Culture last year.

Most of the others were invented for less gentle purposes: we have a nasty-looking flamethrower on wheels meant to breach stone fortresses; a “machine gun” able to fire arrows much more rapidly than any bowman; a nine-story-tall proto-tank fully stocked with catapults and soldiers ready to swarm a city; and a gigantic claw, designed by no less a mind than Archimedes, able to grab and overturn invading warships. Yet as formidable as they sound, evidence of just how all these machines of war worked — and just how well they functioned in actual battle — remains scarce.

Much clearer are records of the Diolkos , recently mentioned here when we featured the megaprojects that even ancient Rome couldn’t pull off . Among those endeavors was a canal across the Isthmus of Corinth, which would save ships having to take the long way around the Peloponnesian peninsula. Or rather, it would save them having to be dragged by a couple hundred slaves over the Diolkos , a paved trackway built in the sixth century BC. Using ramps and winches, ships could be shifted onto a wheeled cart that ran in grooves the whole way, making the whole system a precursor of the railroad, or perhaps an inverted ancestor of the ferry still used to transport railway cars across the Strait of Messina . Like the Romans, the Greeks also considered digging a canal, but to do so might have violated the intentions of Zeus, a better excuse not to build infrastructure than some of those we hear in the twenty-first century.

The Psychedelic Animated Video for Kraftwerk’s “Autobahn” (1979)
Ah, yes, “Autobahn.” From the moment the door slams and the ignition starts, prog rockers and pre-new wavers know a journey is afoot.

Ah, yes, “Autobahn.” From the moment the door slams and the ignition starts, prog rockers and pre-new wavers know a journey is afoot. Though Kraftwerk had already made three albums, and the band members still looked like well-meaning, bookish hippies, 1974’s “Autobahn” is considered Year Zero for the denizens of the Electric Café, the four German robots who made human music with machines.

This cel-drawn animation by Roger Mainwood was made in 1979 to promote “Autobahn,” after most of the culture had caught up with the song, and it’s now bopping around pop culture again. By that last year of the ’70s, Omni magazine was a year old, music was sifting through the shockwaves left by Bowie’s Low and Heroes , analog was flirting with digital, and the world was ready to drive on that long, electric highway.

Mainwood’s protagonist is part alien, part human, and he begins looking around in awe in his hip goggles, then sets off for a run straight out of a Muybridge loop, only to wind up floating, flying, sailing and swimming through a landscape indebted to Peter Max, Push Pin Studios, underground comix, and 1930s modernism.

Mainwood had just graduated from London’s Royal College of Art Film and Television School, and was commissioned by John Halas, the Hungarian immigrant who became known as the Father of British Animation, for Kraftwerk’s record label. The label wanted to put out one of the first music Laserdiscs. (Halas, by the way, directed a very UPA-influenced short called “Automania” in 1963 ). According to Mainwood, he still doesn’t know if the band liked the short or even if they watched it.

Mainwood avoided any direct representation of driving or automobiles, much to his credit, which may be why the film holds its fascination. The animator continued in his field, winding up a producer of several classics of British animation, including The Snowman and the chilling When the Wind Blows . As for the meaning of “Autobahn,” we’ll let Mainwood have the last word:

Thinking back to my thought processes at that time, I remember wanting to specifically not have conventional cars in the film. I wanted a sense of a repetitive journey, and alienation, which I took to be what the music was about…hence the solitary futuristic figure, protected by large goggles, moving through and trying to connect with the journey he is taking. The automobile “monsters” are deliberately threatening (I have never been a big fan of cars or motorways!) and when our “hero” tries to make human contact (with different coloured clones of himself) he can never do it. In the end he realises he is making the repetitive and circular journey alone but strides forward purposefully at the end as he did in the beginning. All of which sounds rather pretentious…but I was a young thing in those days!

When Jorge Luis Borges Co-Wrote a Surreal Sci-Fi Noir Film: Invasión (1969)
“La ciudad es más que la gente.” So declares a character called Don Porfirio in Invasión, the debut feature by Argentine director Hugo Santiago. The line is the film’s most memorable, not…

“ La ciudad es más que la gente. ” So declares a character called Don Porfirio in Invasión , the debut feature by Argentine director Hugo Santiago. The line is the film’s most memorable, not least because of the reversal it pulls on our expectations. Saying that a city is really its people must have been a somewhat banal observation even in 1969, when Invasión came out, but saying that a city is more than its people still sounds contrarian enough to be intriguing. It’s even more compelling coming from Don Porfirio, a mastermind whose intensely abstracted manner and refined literary diction will remind some viewers of no figure so much as Jorge Luis Borges — and as well he might, since Borges co-wrote the script.

Another major contributor to Invasión ’s screenplay was Borges’ longtime friend, occasional collaborator, and junior colleague in letters Adolfo Bioy Casares . Anyone who’s read about their relationship (as detailed in Bioy Casares’ tome of published diaries, simply titled Borges ) knows how deeply entangled it was with the streets of Buenos Aires, where both of them were born and raised. And anyone who knows Buenos Aires will recognize those streets onscreen in this film, despite the title card that calls it Aquilea. Echoing the name of Achilles, it offers a clue as to Borges and Bioy Casares’ classical inspiration for this project, which transposes the city under siege of Homer’s Troy into mid-century Latin America, where a small group of resistance members organize against an arriving army of menacing white-coated invaders.

Though Borges wasn’t exactly one for topicality in his own ficciones , it wouldn’t be wholly unreasonable to make an allegorical reading of the film. It’s set in the year 1957, when Argentina was ruled by Pedro Eugenio Aramburu, one of several dictators in the country’s twentieth-century history. It came out during the dictatorship of Juan Carlos Onganía Carballo. And the 1976 military coup that put Jorge Rafael Videla in power banished it to an official non-existence, seen only in the most underground screenings. It wasn’t until the nineteen-nineties that Invasión was rediscovered and made whole out of partial prints found in France, the country to which Santiago had long since decamped. Now it can be seen on YouTube in one version with optional English and French subtitles, and another, higher resolution version with French subtitles only.

Viewers today may be quick to notice the obvious budgetary limitations, manifest in odd-sounding foley work and theatrical death scenes, but the cinematic vitality of its mixture of film noir, Nouvelle Vague , political thriller, and even science fiction remains undeniable. (With the chases and explosions it manages, it may even partially qualify as an action movie.) So does the atmosphere of the real locations — the streets Borges and Bioy Casares walked, as well as cafés, rail yards, and the climactic football stadium — that constitute its alternately stately and desolate setting. It would be clichéd to say that the city itself becomes a character, but it would also prompt us to ask, which city, Buenos Aires or Aquilea? As with so many other questions about Invasión , there is no one answer.

Watch Accurate Recreations of Medieval Italian Longsword Fighting Techniques, All Based on a Manuscript from…
Given recent history, the prospect of hundreds of young men meeting on Facebook, then traveling from around the country to a central U.S. location might sound like reasonable cause for…

Given recent history, the prospect of hundreds of young men meeting on Facebook, then traveling from around the country to a central U.S. location might sound like reasonable cause for alarm. Yet a convention fitting that description had nothing to do with political violence but, rather, a celebration and appreciation of the name “Josh” (full disclosure: this writer did not attend). The gathering of the Joshes in April 2021 in Nebraska could not have been more peaceful, including its finishing battle royale, conducted with pool noodles.

The Joshes had no concern for proper pool-noodle-wielding technique, if there is such a thing. But groups of people who gather around the country to stage medieval-style battles in live-action role playing (LARP) games with weapons both real and fake might benefit from pointers.

So, too, might those who choreograph sword fights on stage and screen. Where can serious historical re-creators learn how to wield a real blade in historically accurate combat? One resource can be found at Wiktenauer , a wiki devoted to collecting “all of the primary and secondary source literature that makes up the text of historical European Martial arts (HEMA) research.”

The Fior di Battaglia (“Flower of Battle”) —an Italian fencing manual by Fiore de’i Liberi dating from circa 1404—offers richly- and copiously-illustrated demonstrations of medieval Italian longsword fighting techniques. In the original manuscript, seen here and at The Getty , “the illustrations are inked sketches with gold leafing on the crowns and garters,” notes the Wiktenauer entry. They dominate the text, which “takes the form of descriptive paragraphs set in poor Italian verse, which are nevertheless fairly clear and informative.” So clear, indeed, the brooding young men of Akademia Szermierzy—a Polish group that recreates medieval sword-fighting techniques—can more than convincingly mimic the moves in the video at the top.

Once they get going, after some requisite pre-fight rigmarole, it’s impressive stuff, maybe already familiar to modern fencers and certain members of the Society for Creative Anachronism , the LARP-ing organization of amateurs recreating everything from the Middle Ages and the Renaissance. But for those who think all live-action role-playing is the equivalent of the Battle of the Joshes (or off-brand Nazis running through the streets in homemade armor), the sheer ballet of historical sword-fighting may come as a surprise — and maybe inspire a few more people to pull on the doublet and hose.
